content: Foot-and-mouth disease (FMD), also known by its Latin name Aphtae epizooticae, is a highly contagious viral disease that primarily affects cattle and pigs. It can also infect other cloven-hoofed animals, such as deer, goats, and sheep, as well as certain non-cloven-hoofed species like elephants, rats, and hedgehogs. However, humans are rarely affected by this disease. The causative agent of FMD is the foot-and-mouth disease virus (FMDV), which belongs to the Aphthovirus genus within the Picornaviridae family. This virus is responsible for an acute systemic vesicular disease that impacts livestock globally. FMDV is highly variable and extremely transmissible. The viral nature of FMD was first identified in 1897 by Friedrich Loeffler. He demonstrated this by passing the blood of an infected animal through a fine porcelain filter, which removed bacteria but allowed the virus to pass through. The filtered fluid retained the ability to cause disease in healthy animals, confirming the viral etiology of FMD. The pathophysiology of FMD begins when the virus comes into contact with a host cell. It binds to specific receptor sites on the cell surface, triggering the cell membrane to fold inward and engulf the virus. Once inside the host cell, the virus sheds its protein coat, releasing its genetic material. The viral RNA then hijacks the host cell's machinery to produce large quantities of new viral RNA and protein components. These components are assembled into new virus particles. Eventually, the host cell bursts (a process known as lysis), releasing the newly formed viruses, which can then infect additional cells. FMD is caused by FMDV, a member of the Aphthovirus genus in the Picornaviridae family. These viruses are small, measuring approximately 25-30 nanometers in diameter, and are non-enveloped with an icosahedral structure. Their genetic material consists of single-stranded RNA. There are seven distinct serotypes of FMDV: O, A, C, SAT-1, SAT-2, SAT-3, and Asia-1. These serotypes exhibit some geographic specificity, with the O serotype being the most prevalent worldwide. FMD is a disease of significant global concern due to its wide host range and rapid transmission. While some countries have successfully eradicated FMD, it remains endemic in many regions, posing a persistent threat to international livestock industries. The incubation period for FMD typically ranges from 3 to 8 days. The disease manifests with a high fever, which subsides after two to three days. Affected animals develop blisters (vesicles) inside the mouth, leading to excessive salivation and drooling. Similar blisters may form on the feet, which can rupture and result in lameness. Adult animals often experience weight loss, which may take several months to recover. In male animals, swelling of the testicles can occur, while in lactating cows, milk production may decline significantly.
